reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Full-thickness (complete) rectal prolapse is protrusion of the entire rectal wall through the anus, with concentric mucosal folds, whereas mucosal prolapse and internal intussusception are distinct, less severe entities
It is most common in older women and in children, and is frequently associated with chronic straining, pelvic floor weakness, and a redundant sigmoid colon
Typical symptoms are a protruding mass on defecation, mucous discharge, bleeding, and a sensation of incomplete evacuation, with faecal incontinence in a large proportion
The diagnosis is often made by asking the patient to strain, ideally on a commode, to reproduce the prolapse; concentric rings distinguish it from the radial folds of prolapsing haemorrhoids
Defecating proctography or dynamic MRI can demonstrate internal intussusception and associated pelvic floor abnormalities when clinical findings are equivocal
Coexisting incontinence and constipation should be assessed, and colonic evaluation is prudent to exclude a lead point or synchronous pathology

Definitive treatment is surgical and is broadly divided into abdominal approaches (rectopexy, with or without resection) and perineal procedures, chosen according to fitness, symptoms, and surgeon preference
reference.pathophysiology: Full-thickness rectal prolapse is understood as a circumferential intussusception of the rectum that progresses until the bowel protrudes through the anal canal. Contributing factors include a deep rectovaginal or rectovesical pouch, loss of the normal posterior rectal fixation, a redundant mobile rectosigmoid, weak pelvic floor and anal sphincter musculature, and chronically raised intra-abdominal pressure from straining. Repeated prolapse stretches and damages the pudendal nerves and sphincter complex, which explains the frequent association with faecal incontinence, while chronic mucosal exposure produces discharge, bleeding, and ulceration.
additionalDifferentials: Anal or perianal skin tags or condylomata
additionalInvestigations: Examination with the patient straining to reproduce the prolapse
Colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy to exclude a lead-point lesion or synchronous colorectal pathology
Defecating proctography or dynamic pelvic MRI for internal intussusception and pelvic floor assessment
Anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound when incontinence is prominent
Colonic transit studies where significant constipation coexists
redFlags: Irreducible, incarcerated prolapse with congestion, ulceration, or impending strangulation requiring urgent reduction or surgery
Significant bleeding or a palpable mass suggesting an underlying tumour
Acute large prolapse in a frail patient with obstruction
reference.prognosis: Surgical repair relieves the prolapse in most patients with acceptable recurrence rates that vary by procedure, and continence often improves over time though it may not fully recover if pelvic floor and nerve damage is longstanding. Constipation can persist or occasionally worsen, and outcomes are best when associated functional problems are addressed alongside the anatomical repair.
pitfalls: Confusing full-thickness prolapse with prolapsing haemorrhoids and offering inappropriate treatment
Failing to reproduce the prolapse on examination and therefore missing or underestimating it
Not excluding a colorectal neoplasm acting as a lead point before elective repair
Ignoring coexisting incontinence or constipation, leading to poor functional results despite anatomical success
Delaying intervention in an incarcerated or ischaemic prolapse
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Definitive treatment is surgical repair, either abdominal rectopexy (increasingly ventral mesh rectopexy) or a perineal procedure such as Delorme or Altemeier in frail patients
Optimise bowel habit with fibre, fluids and laxatives to reduce straining before and after surgery
Manually reduce an incarcerated prolapse, using topical sugar to shrink oedema, with urgent surgery if it is irreducible or strangulated
Assess and manage coexisting faecal incontinence and constipation, including pelvic-floor biofeedback
Exclude a lead-point lesion with colonic evaluation before repair
Multidisciplinary colorectal and pelvic-floor input, with monitoring for recurrence and persistent bowel dysfunction after repair
